lesson_title: A Cent a Day, Doubled: Exponents in the Real World
hook_text: R1 000 a day for a month, or one cent doubled every day? Most people pick wrong. Here is why.
clip_script: R1 000 a day for 30 days is R30 000. Now the cent: one cent, doubled every day. Day two, 2 cents. Day ten, about 5 rand. Looks hopeless. But 2 to the power 10 is about a thousand, so every ten days multiplies by a thousand. Day 30 is a thousand times a thousand times a thousand cents — a billion cents, ten million rand. That is what an exponent does: slow, slow, then it runs away. Same thing with bacteria: 500 cells doubling every hour for six hours is 500 times 2 to the sixth, 32 000 — not 500 times 2 times 6. Every time a problem says every, each or per, you are looking at a power. Spot it, write it, and let the exponent do the counting.
visual_style: A split screen: a flat stack of R1 000 notes growing steadily on the left, a single cent on the right that barely moves for ten days then explodes past the frame with a counter spinning to ten million.
pacing: Slow build for the first beats, then a sudden rush as the doubling takes off.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never underestimate a doubling again.
